u0/how-the-lsat-works.prompt: Which sections count toward your 120–180 score on the current four-section LSAT?

choices.A: One Logical Reasoning section and two Reading Comprehension sections
choices.B: Two Logical Reasoning sections, one Reading Comprehension section and the Argumentative Writing sample
choices.C: Two Logical Reasoning sections and one Reading Comprehension section
choices.D: One section each of Logical Reasoning, Reading Comprehension and Logic Games

why.A: Reversed. Logical Reasoning is two of the three scored sections, about two-thirds of the score.
why.B: The writing sample is unscored. Schools read it, but it is not part of the 120–180.
why.C: Right. Two scored LR, one scored RC, plus one unscored variable section that can appear anywhere.
why.D: Logic Games were removed from the LSAT in August 2024 and are gone for good.

u0/how-the-lsat-works.prompt: Forty seconds remain in a section and three questions are still blank. What does the scoring rule say to do?

choices.A: Answer all three, even as guesses, because a wrong answer costs nothing
choices.B: Leave them blank, because a wrong answer costs more than a blank
choices.C: Answer only the ones where you can eliminate at least two choices
choices.D: Spend the time checking an earlier answer instead, since guesses rarely land

why.A: Right. Every question is worth one raw point and there is no penalty for guessing, so never leave a blank.
why.B: There is no guessing penalty. A blank scores the same as a wrong answer, and a guess has a chance of scoring.
why.C: Elimination helps, but even a blind guess beats a blank when wrong answers cost nothing.
why.D: Checking may be worth something, but not at the cost of leaving three questions blank.

u0/how-the-lsat-works.prompt: On recent forms, about how many questions can you miss and still score 175?

why.A: A perfect or near-perfect test is a 180, not a 175.
why.B: One miss is closer to 180 on recent forms.
why.C: About twelve misses lands in the mid-160s, below 170 (about eight misses).
why.D: Right. Four or five misses out of about 77, roughly one and a half per section. The goal is to stop losing points you already know how to earn.

u0/how-the-lsat-works.prompt: Which review habit does the lesson single out as what top scorers can do?

choices.A: Name the exact word that makes each wrong answer wrong
choices.B: Take more full practice tests than anyone else
choices.C: Diagram every stimulus before reading the answer choices
choices.D: Reread the explanation for every question they got right

why.A: Right. That precision is what this program's review step trains: every miss is tagged with why, and comes back until the pattern is gone.
why.B: Volume helps only up to a point; the lesson's emphasis is on how you review, not how many tests you take.
why.C: The lesson says plainly that the program does not diagram every stimulus.
why.D: Reviewing right answers can help, but it is not the habit the lesson names.

u0/how-the-lsat-works.prompt: What changes from the August 2027 LSAT onward?

choices.A: Logic Games return as a scored section
choices.B: Reading Comprehension comes first, and the unscored questions are mixed into all three sections
choices.C: The number of scored questions rises and the score scale changes
choices.D: The Argumentative Writing sample becomes part of the scored test

why.A: Logic Games are not coming back.
why.B: Right. RC first (52 minutes), then two LR sections (45 minutes each), breaks after the first two sections, and no separate unscored section.

u0/how-this-program-works.prompt: You answer a level-2 question correctly in 7 seconds and mark it “sure.” What happens to your skill rating?

choices.A: It rises more than usual, because you were fast and sure
choices.B: It rises by the normal amount for a level-2 question
choices.C: It falls slightly, because answering that fast counts as rushing
choices.D: Nothing; answers under 10 seconds don’t count toward the rating

why.A: Speed and confidence don’t earn extra rating. Very fast answers are left out altogether.
why.B: It would, at 10 seconds or more. Under 10 seconds the answer is not counted.
why.C: A correct answer never lowers the rating; a very fast one is simply ignored.
why.D: Right. Answers under 10 seconds, and answers marked guess, are left out so lucky hits can’t inflate your rating.

u0/how-this-program-works.prompt: You missed a question fast and confidently, by picking the answer that reversed the argument’s logic. Which cause and cure fit?

choices.A: Misread: slow down the first read and reread the stem
choices.B: Logic gap: go back to the lesson and drill the pattern untimed
choices.C: Time pressure: work on pacing checkpoints and skip rules
choices.D: Careless: trust your first read unless you can prove a switch

why.A: Right. Fast, confident and wrong, with the reversed answer picked, is the lesson’s description of a misread.
why.B: A logic gap is not seeing the structure. Here the structure was readable; the read itself was too quick.
why.C: Time pressure shows up as guessing or bailing, not a fast confident pick.
why.D: Careless means switching off a right answer. You never had the right answer here.

u0/how-this-program-works.prompt: After you tag a miss in the Review Inbox, when does it come back?

choices.A: The next day, and then not again
choices.B: After 3, 5 and then 10 days, paired with a fresh question of the same shape, until you’ve beaten the pattern three times
choices.C: Once a week for as long as you use the app
choices.D: Only when you choose to reopen it yourself

why.A: One return is not enough to prove the pattern is gone.
why.B: Right. Spaced returns, each with a fresh question of the same shape, until the pattern is beaten three times.
why.C: The schedule widens and then stops once the pattern is beaten; it isn’t weekly forever.
why.D: Re-drilling is automatic: due misses are served first in drills.

u0/how-this-program-works.prompt: According to the lesson, what is the drill really scored on?

choices.A: The percentage of questions you get right
choices.B: Whether your “sure” answers are right and whether your misses stop repeating
choices.C: How fast you answer each question
choices.D: How many questions you answer each day

why.A: A raw percentage doesn’t tell you what to fix; the lesson says so directly.
why.B: Right. Calibrated confidence and misses that stop repeating are the two things that move the score.
why.C: Speed comes later, once the method is reliable.
why.D: Volume without review is what keeps people stuck.

u0/how-this-program-works.prompt: Your displayed rating for a question type is about 75. What does that mean?

choices.A: You get about 75% of that type right
choices.B: You are at the 75th percentile of test takers
choices.C: You are reliable through level-3 questions of that type
choices.D: You are close to acing that type

why.A: The rating is not a percentage correct; it measures the difficulty you handle reliably.
why.B: It is not a percentile against other test takers.
why.C: Right. Around 75 on the 0–100 scale means reliable through level 3.

u0/how-to-study.prompt: Which two study techniques does the lesson call the most effective measured?

choices.B: Timed full tests from day one and daily score tracking

why.A: The lesson puts these far behind practice testing and spacing.
why.B: Timing too early teaches you to guess faster; the lesson says accuracy first.
why.C: Not the two the lesson names.
why.D: Right. The drill is the lesson, and re-drilling a miss days later is where learning compounds.

u0/how-to-study.prompt: When should you move a question type from untimed to timed practice?

choices.A: When your untimed accuracy on level 1–3 questions of that type is above about 85% across the last 20
choices.B: As soon as you finish all the lessons for that type
choices.C: After you have answered 100 questions of that type
choices.D: When your untimed accuracy stops improving

why.A: Right. Before that, a timer measures reading speed, not reasoning.
why.B: Finishing lessons doesn’t show the method is reliable yet.
why.C: Volume isn’t the test; accuracy on recent questions is.
why.D: A plateau calls for better review, not a timer.

u0/how-to-study.prompt: Your timed section score is 9 points below your blind-review score on the same section. What does the gap suggest?

choices.A: Your ceiling is content, so go back to untimed drilling on your weakest types
choices.B: You need to take a full practice test every day
choices.C: You know the material but can’t execute under time: work on pacing, skipping and confidence
choices.D: Nothing; a gap that size is normal and needs no change

why.A: That is the cure for a small or no gap, where blind review doesn’t rescue the score either.
why.B: More full tests without fixing execution repeats the same problem.
why.C: Right. A big gap (8 or more points) means the knowledge is there and the timing is the problem.
why.D: The lesson treats 8 or more points as a big gap with a specific fix.

u0/how-to-study.prompt: Three timed sections in a row land at the same score. What does the lesson say to do first?

choices.A: Double the number of sections you take each week
choices.B: Check the inbox for error tags that keep repeating, and raise review quality while cutting volume
choices.C: Skip ahead to harder material so the scores move
choices.D: Stop drilling and only reread lessons for a week

why.A: Volume is the usual response to a plateau, and the lesson says it is the wrong one.
why.B: Right. Repeating tags show the bottleneck; twenty questions reviewed properly beat sixty rushed.
why.C: Harder material doesn’t fix the repeating cause of the misses.
why.D: The lesson suggests rereading one section, not dropping drills.

u0/how-to-study.prompt: What does the final week before the test look like?

choices.A: A full test every day to build stamina
choices.B: Only the hardest questions, to sharpen up
choices.C: New lessons on any question type you skipped
choices.D: One full test at your test time the weekend before, light level 1–2 drilling, error-journal rereads, and nothing the day before

why.A: The final week protects the score; daily full tests wear you out.
